1449## ask-the-record
1450
1451
1452ask-the-record is a question box for a personal site, a documentation page or a project page that never writes an answer. Every reply is a quote from your own content, word for word, with the matching words marked, the strength of the match shown, and a link to where it came from. When nothing in the content supports an answer, it says "No source for that." and shows the numbers behind that decision. Retrieval runs in the visitor's browser, so their question never leaves the page. A generated answer has to be checked against its source; a quote is the source, so a reader can check it in one click.
1453
1454### Quickstart
1455
1456You need Node.js 22 or later. From a clone of this repository:
1457
1458```sh
1459npm ci
1460npm run build
1461npm run demo
1462```
1463
1464Then open http://127.0.0.1:4310/ to ask this README questions. The page shows this file line by line, as its own source. Asking a question marks the passage that answers it in place, writes the question in the margin beside it, and places the question on a map of the README's facts. The demo's record is built from this file, so it can only answer what is written here. The demo also takes your own markdown: choose "Use your own markdown", paste a page, and the record is built, embedded and searched in your browser, with nothing uploaded. The docs page, at http://127.0.0.1:4310/docs/, lists every attribute, event and part next to a live specimen.
1465
1466To put a question box on your own page, build a record from your markdown. The repository has a small example about page to try it on:
1467
1468```sh
1469node dist/cli.js build examples/about.md -o examples/record.json --embed
1470node dist/cli.js ask examples/record.json "Which street is the studio on?"
1471node dist/cli.js ask examples/record.json --hybrid "Can I park there?"
1472```
1473
1474With npm run demo still running, http://127.0.0.1:4310/examples/ shows that record in a page with nothing else on it. The whole integration is two lines of HTML:
1475
1476```html
1477<script type="module" src="ask-the-record.min.js"></script>
1478<ask-the-record src="record.json"></ask-the-record>
1479```
1480
1481When the page also uses the map or the ranks view, the script loads ask-the-record-explain.min.js from beside itself, so the embed stays one script tag.
1482
1483For your own page, build from your own markdown and copy dist/ask-the-record.min.js and the record next to the page. The package is not published to npm yet, so these commands run the built CLI from the clone.
1484
1485The --embed flag downloads the embedding model once (about 24 MB) and runs it on your machine. Without --embed, the record still works: keyword search is instant, and the browser embeds the facts itself once the model has loaded.
1486
1487### How it works
1488
1489A record is your markdown, split into facts. Each fact is one sentence, list item, table row or short code block, with the section it sits in and the line it starts on. The fact keeps the exact text a reader sees, with the markdown syntax removed and nothing reworded.
1490
1491The build step parses the markdown, gives every fact a stable id, and writes record.json. A fact's id is its section's anchor plus a hash of its text, so it survives edits to the sentences around it. Identical sentences in one section are told apart by number, in order. With --embed, every fact is embedded with all-MiniLM-L6-v2 and stored as 384 signed bytes, and a t-SNE layout of the facts is computed for the optional map.
1492
1493When the page loads, the element fetches record.json and validates it before using any of it. Validation checks the schema and the record's own consistency: references in range, ids unique, vectors of the right size, and embeddings built for exactly these facts. An invalid record is reported as an error, never answered from.
1494
1495Keyword search works as soon as the record has loaded. Keyword search uses BM25 over English words, with stop words removed and Porter stemming, so "refusal" matches "refuses". Section titles and table headings count at half weight, so a fact is found by the heading it sits under. Code blocks also count at half weight, with each word counted once, because code repeats its keywords.
1496
1497Meaning search starts when the visitor first focuses the question box. A Web Worker loads transformers.js and the model, tries WebGPU first and WebAssembly second, and trusts a backend only after it reproduces two of the record's stored vectors to a cosine of at least 0.95. In testing in Chromium, WebAssembly and WebGPU reproduced them to cosines between 0.985 and 0.993. After that, only the question is embedded; comparing it with every fact is a single pass of dot products. A model that is already running is checked the same way before it serves a different record.
1498
1499The two rankings are combined by reciprocal rank fusion with k = 10. A fact's fused score is the sum of 1 / (k + rank) over the keyword ranking and the meaning ranking.
1500
1501The refusal policy then decides whether anything supports an answer. The policy answers on meaning when the closest fact has a cosine of at least 0.48. The policy answers on keywords when one fact holds at least 60% of the question's words, weighted by how rare each word is, and that same fact has a cosine of at least 0.30. The meaning bar rises by 0.08 when the question uses a word the record never does. In every other case it refuses and says which number fell short.
1502
1503When typing pauses, the box previews the answer it would give; pressing Enter asks, and only an asked question is announced or refused.
1504
1505An answer is up to three facts, quoted verbatim, best first. When the answer rests on meaning, each quoted fact needs a cosine within 0.10 of the closest fact, or the question's keywords and a cosine of at least 0.30. When it rests on keywords, each quoted fact needs both. The words that matched the question are marked, and words that matched through a configured synonym are marked differently. Each quote shows its section, a similarity score or the count of matched words, and a link to its source.
1506
1507After a meaning answer, the box shows which words the match leaned on. Each quoted fact is embedded again with one word removed at a time, and the words whose removal costs the most similarity are underlined, more heavily the more they cost. The underline measures the model's sensitivity to a word, which is evidence for a reader to weigh, not an explanation of the model.
1508
1509Without a --source URL, quotes link to the section's anchor on the page that hosts the box. With --source, quotes link to that page, and a text fragment scrolls to and highlights the quoted sentence itself.
1510
1511### Answers that prove themselves
1512
1513Quoting is the default, and it stays instant. On top of it, <ask-the-record-verify for="ask"> writes an answer in its own words and then proves each sentence against the record, in the browser, sentence by sentence, as the answer is written. A sentence the record does not back is struck out where it stands, with its score, and an answer with nothing left standing becomes a refusal.
1514
1515The writer is Qwen2.5 0.5B Instruct, a small open instruct model. The writer reads the four source lines the quotes came from and writes two or three sentences. The checker is DeBERTa-v3 xsmall, a natural language inference (NLI) model trained on SNLI and MultiNLI, which scores whether one text entails, contradicts or is neutral to another. The checker runs in a second worker, so every sentence is checked as soon as it is finished, while the next is still being written.
1516
1517Each sentence is compared with the six retrieved record sentences that share most of its words, and with the whole paragraph of the best of them, and the best entailment counts. That comparison against each premise sentence is the zero-shot method of SummaC (Laban et al. 2022). Support is looked for among the retrieved passages, as in the research step of RARR (Gao et al. 2023), rather than taken from the model's own citations, because a model this small cites unreliably. Using NLI to judge whether a sentence is attributable to its source follows AIS (Rashkin et al. 2023) and TRUE (Honovich et al. 2022). Scoring an answer sentence by sentence, against hand labels, follows FActScore (Min et al. 2023); answering with attributions is the setting of Attributed QA (Bohnet et al. 2022).
1518
1519A sentence stands only when its best entailment is at least 0.90 and beats contradiction against the same record sentence. A sentence a record sentence contradicts is marked as contradicted, and any other unsupported sentence as unsupported. A sentence too short to stand alone, such as "Yes", is shown but never counted as an answer. Each kept sentence links to the line that supports it, and with highlight set, that record sentence is underlined in the page.
1520
1521The two models are 889 MB together: 793 MB for the writer and 96 MB for the checker. Nothing is downloaded until the visitor asks, and the size is shown before the download starts. Progress is shown as it goes, and the download can be cancelled at any moment. A failed download is reported in plain words, and the quotes keep answering. The weights stay in the browser's Cache API, so a second visit downloads nothing; with cache="none" they are kept for one visit only. The writer runs on WebGPU when its backend passes a check, and on WebAssembly otherwise, which is much slower. On a phone, the box offers the download with a warning, and the recorded runs still play.
1522
1523Until the models are loaded, recorded runs of this same code are replayed at the speed they ran, and labelled as recorded. npm run verify:record records them in headless Chromium, and the demo's five suggested questions are chosen to show each outcome.
1524
1525#### Measured
1526
1527npm run verify:record -- --eval writes an answer for every question in the evaluation set and records every token and score. Each sentence the writer drafted was then labelled once, by hand, as supported by this README or not. A sentence counts as supported only if every part of it is in the README, so one wrong number or one added claim makes it unsupported. The builder of this repository (Claude, an AI assistant) did the labelling, before looking at the checker's verdicts. The labels are in eval/verify-labels.json, each with its exact sentence, for anyone to audit. The entailment bar was chosen on the development half alone, from 0.5 to 0.95, as the one whose kept sentences were most often truly supported. The held-out half was scored once the bar was fixed. npm run verify:score reproduces the table; two other checkers were scored on the very same sentences with npm run verify:rescore. The percentages are followed by their counts and 95% Wilson intervals.
1528
1529Checker, half · Sentences supported, unchecked · Sentences supported, after checking · Supported sentences kept · Answerable, answered with support · Unanswerable, refused
1530|---|---|---|---|---|---|
1531nli-deberta-v3-xsmall (bar 0.90), development · 13% (4/30; 5–30) · 33% (3/9; 12–65) · 75% (3/4; 30–95) · 13% (2/15; 4–38) · 82% (9/11; 52–95)
1532nli-deberta-v3-xsmall (bar 0.90), held out · 13% (4/30; 5–30) · 100% (3/3; 44–100) · 75% (3/4; 30–95) · 13% (2/15; 4–38) · 100% (11/11; 74–100)
1533DeBERTa-v3-xsmall-mnli-fever-anli-ling-binary (bar 0.95), development · 13% (4/30; 5–30) · 33% (1/3; 6–79) · 25% (1/4; 5–70) · 7% (1/15; 1–30) · 91% (10/11; 62–98)
1534DeBERTa-v3-xsmall-mnli-fever-anli-ling-binary (bar 0.95), held out · 13% (4/30; 5–30) · 100% (3/3; 44–100) · 75% (3/4; 30–95) · 13% (2/15; 4–38) · 100% (11/11; 74–100)
1535DeBERTa-v3-base-mnli-fever-anli (bar 0.95), development · 13% (4/30; 5–30) · 30% (3/10; 11–60) · 75% (3/4; 30–95) · 20% (3/15; 7–45) · 91% (10/11; 62–98)
1536DeBERTa-v3-base-mnli-fever-anli (bar 0.95), held out · 13% (4/30; 5–30) · 43% (3/7; 16–75) · 75% (3/4; 30–95) · 13% (2/15; 4–38) · 73% (8/11; 43–90)
1537
1538The writer is the weak part: unchecked, only 8 of the 60 sentences it drafted are supported by the README. With the checker, 3 of the 9 sentences kept on the development half were supported, and 3 of the 3 kept on the held-out half; 20 of the 22 unanswerable questions were refused. The sentences it wrongly kept change a number slightly (795 MB for 793 MB), lift a phrase of the README out of context, or misread a passage. Neither of the other two checkers did better on the held-out half, and the larger one, DeBERTa-v3 base, kept more unsupported sentences there. The counts are small, so the intervals are wide, and most answerable questions end in a refusal: the checker trades answers for being right.
1539
1540### Using the element
1541
1542The element is <ask-the-record>, a framework-free custom element that renders into Shadow DOM.
1543
1544Attribute · Meaning
1545|---|---|
1546src · URL of the record.json to load. Required.
1547model · Embedding model id, or none for keyword search only. Defaults to the model the record was embedded with.
1548model-host · Base URL for model files, for self-hosting. Defaults to the Hugging Face Hub.
1549model-dtype · Model weights to load when the record has no embeddings. Defaults to q8.
1550runtime · URL of the transformers.js ES module. Defaults to a pinned version on jsDelivr.
1551live · Preview answers while the visitor types. Previews are never announced or refused.
1552label · Visible label for the question box. Defaults to "Ask a question".
1553placeholder · Placeholder text for the question box.
1554highlight · A CSS selector. Each answer is also marked inside the element it names, using the CSS Custom Highlight API.
1555highlight-scroll · With highlight, scroll the first quote into view.
1556
1557With model="none", the element makes no requests beyond record.json. A change to model, model-host, model-dtype or runtime takes effect at once, without fetching the record again.
1558
1559Anything placed in the element's suggestions slot, such as example questions, is shown between the status line and the answer.
1560
1561The element's ask(question) method puts a question in the box, asks it, and resolves with the result. Given a vector, as in ask(question, { vector }), the element uses that embedding instead of running the model; the vector must come from the record's own model. A supplied vector is refused when the record has no stored vectors, when its size is wrong, or when the facts are being searched with vectors that another model computed in the browser. The demo embeds its suggested questions when the page is built, so its first answer needs no download. The element's load(record) method takes a record object instead of fetching src, validates it exactly as a fetched one, and throws on an invalid record. A record built in the page has no vectors, so the model the element is already running embeds its facts in the browser.
1562
1563dist/ask-the-record-build.min.js is the markdown parser and the quotability linter for the browser, about 23 KB gzipped, for pages that let visitors try their own content. The demo loads it only when someone does.
1564
1565The element's record, result, modelState and diagnostics properties expose what it loaded, what it answered and how the model was checked. The element's thresholds property overrides the refusal policy, which you should do when you use a different embedding model.
1566
1567The element dispatches these events, all of which bubble out of the Shadow DOM:
1568
1569Event · When
1570|---|---|
1571ask-the-record:ready · The record has loaded and validated. detail.record is the record.
1572ask-the-record:status · The model's state changed. detail.text is the status line shown.
1573ask-the-record:answer · A question was answered or refused. detail.result is the full result. An empty question is ignored.
1574ask-the-record:preview · With live, a preview was shown while typing. detail.result is the result.
1575ask-the-record:vectors · The facts of a record without vectors were embedded in the browser. detail.vectors holds them.
1576ask-the-record:located · With highlight, an answer was looked for in the page. detail.located lists each quote found, with its Range; detail.highlighted is false where the Highlight API is missing.
1577ask-the-record:leans · Attribution finished. detail.leans maps each quote to the words its meaning match leaned on.
1578ask-the-record:clear · The answer on show was cleared, by Escape or an emptied box.
1579ask-the-record:source · A quote's source link was clicked. Call preventDefault() to handle it yourself.
1580ask-the-record:error · The record could not be loaded, or asking failed unexpectedly. detail.error is the error.
1581
1582The element inherits the page's font and text colour. Every colour is derived from the page's own text colour unless you set it. You can restyle it with these CSS custom properties: --atr-accent, --atr-color, --atr-muted, --atr-rule, --atr-mark, --atr-mark-related, --atr-font, --atr-quote-font, --atr-mono-font, --atr-input-size, --atr-quote-size, --atr-gap and --atr-focus.
1583
1584For anything else, every piece is exposed with ::part(): form, label, field, input, submit, status, load, answer, summary, quotes, quote, quote-context, quote-text, passage, code, mark, lean, legend, pending, quote-meta, source, strength, strength-label, meter, meter-fill, meter-mark, refusal, refusal-title, refusal-reason, closest and error.
1585
1586The question box has a visible label, and Enter asks the question. Escape clears the box and the answer. Each answer or refusal is announced through a polite live region: the number of quotes and the first quote, or the refusal and its reason. Every link in an answer is reachable with the Tab key. Animation is skipped when the visitor prefers reduced motion, and marks stay visible in Windows high-contrast mode.
1587
1588#### Written answers, checked
1589
1590<ask-the-record-verify for="ask"> follows the <ask-the-record id="ask"> it names, like the map. The verify element's attributes are recordings (a JSON file of recorded runs to replay), model-host and runtime (to host the models and transformers.js yourself), cache="none", and highlight (a selector: each supporting record sentence is underlined there). The element's start() loads the models and cancel() stops a download or a run at once. The element dispatches ask-the-record-verify:state, ask-the-record-verify:sentence (each verdict, with its line), ask-the-record-verify:cite (a line number was followed) and ask-the-record-verify:done. The file is dist/ask-the-record-verify.min.js, about 20 KB gzipped, and the single script loads it when the page uses the element.
1591
1592#### Marking answers in the page
1593
1594With highlight="#article", every answer is also marked inside the element that selector names, without adding any markup: the quoted passages, the question's words in them, and, once attribution has run, the words the meaning match leaned on. A refusal marks its closest passage instead. Each mark is a named highlight for the page to style: ::highlight(ask-the-record), ::highlight(ask-the-record-words), ::highlight(ask-the-record-leans) and ::highlight(ask-the-record-closest). A page that draws its markdown as source lines can mark each line with data-record-line, and then each fact is found on exactly the line it starts on; otherwise a fact is looked for in its section, by heading id. To make the page the only place an answer shows, hide the element's own answer with ask-the-record::part(answer) { display: none; }. The demo works that way.
1595
1596#### The map and the ranks
1597
1598<ask-the-record-map for="ask"> draws the record as points, one per fact, next to the <ask-the-record id="ask"> it names. With a record built using --embed, facts are placed by meaning, using a t-SNE layout computed at build time; otherwise they are grouped by section. When a question is answered, the quoted facts are marked, so you can see where in the record the answer came from. A t-SNE layout cannot place a new point exactly, so the question is drawn at the centre of its five nearest facts by meaning, weighted by similarity squared, with a line to each fact it quoted, and the caption says so. A refused question is drawn outside the cloud, beyond its nearest facts, and further out the further its closest fact fell short of the bar, with dotted lines to its three nearest facts and their scores. For a record of up to 1,000 facts without a layout, such as one built in the page, the map runs t-SNE in the browser once the facts are embedded, a slice per animation frame, and then moves the points to their places by meaning.
1599
1600<ask-the-record-ranks for="ask"> shows how an answer was decided: the facts ranked by shared words (BM25) and by meaning (cosine) side by side, a line joining each fact that appears in both, and the fused order the quotes were taken from. The rankings appear in that order, words first.
1601
1602Both views are in dist/ask-the-record-explain.min.js, which dist/ask-the-record.min.js loads by itself when the page uses either one.
1603
1604#### Privacy and requests
1605
1606The question is never sent anywhere. The question is embedded in a Web Worker on the visitor's device and compared with the record in the page.
1607
1608By default, the model files are downloaded from the Hugging Face Hub and the runtime from jsDelivr, so those services see the visitor's IP address, but never the question. To avoid third-party requests, host the runtime and the model files yourself and set runtime and model-host, or use model="none".
1609
1610The browser caches the model after the first visit. On a connection that asks to save data, the model is not downloaded until the visitor chooses to load it.
1611
1612#### Content Security Policy
1613
1614On a page with a Content Security Policy, the element needs worker-src blob: for its model worker, on top of wherever its script and record.json are served from ('self' on your own site). With the default runtime and model, it also needs script-src https://cdn.jsdelivr.net 'wasm-unsafe-eval' and connect-src https://cdn.jsdelivr.net https://huggingface.co https://*.hf.co. The demo page's whole policy is default-src 'self'; script-src 'self' https://cdn.jsdelivr.net 'wasm-unsafe-eval'; worker-src blob:; connect-src 'self' https://cdn.jsdelivr.net https://huggingface.co https://*.hf.co; style-src 'self'; img-src 'self' data:; object-src 'none'; base-uri 'none'; form-action 'none'. The element's styles are constructed stylesheets, so style-src needs no 'unsafe-inline', and script-src needs no blob:. When the worker is blocked, the element says so and keeps answering by keywords.
1615
1616### The record format
1617
1618The record format is versioned, and this is version 1; the element rejects any other version. The JSON Schema for record.json is in schema/record.schema.json, and every record is checked against it when it is built and when it is loaded.
1619
1620A record holds a title, a language, an optional source URL, optional synonym groups, the sections, and the facts. Each fact has an id, its text, its kind (text, item, row or code), its section, and the line in the markdown it came from. A record built with --embed also holds the model name, the int8 vectors with one scale per fact, and a hash of the exact text that was embedded. A record built with --embed that has between 5 and 3,000 facts also holds the map layout.
1621
1622Facts are quoted exactly as written, so write sentences that stand on their own. A sentence that starts with "It" or "This" reads poorly as a quote, because its subject is in the sentence before.
1623
1624### The command line
1625
1626Command · What it does
1627|---|---|
1628build <record.md> -o <record.json> · Parses markdown into a validated record.
1629check <record.json> · Validates a record and summarises it.
1630lint <record.md> · Reports facts that will read badly as quotes: ones that start with a pronoun, are very short or very long, or repeat.
1631ask <record.json> <question> · Asks a record from the terminal; --hybrid embeds the question too, and --json prints the full result.
1632explain <record.json> <question> · Shows the working: the top facts by fused rank, every score, which were quoted, and why the policy answered or refused.
1633eval <record.json> <questions.json> · Scores a record on your own labelled questions; --min-precision turns it into a check for continuous integration.
1634
1635The explain command shows the working behind an answer. Asked of the example page in examples/, the box finds the sentence that answers a yes-or-no question, even though BM25 cannot see the "not" in it:
1636
1637```text
1638Question Do you build websites?
1639Mode hybrid, Xenova/all-MiniLM-L6-v2
1640
1641 rank quoted cosine keywords bm25 rrf×100 fact
1642 1 yes 0.56 █████▋ 100% ████████ 4.77 18.18 We do not build websites or apps.
1643 Work, line 7
1644 2 0.29 ██▉ 0% 0.00 8.33 We draw printed maps, trail signs and visitor guides.
1645 Work, line 7
1646
1647Answered on meaning: the closest fact's cosine is 0.56, and the bar is 0.48.
1648```
1649
1650A questions file is a JSON list of objects, each with a question and, for questions the record should answer, a support list of passages any one of which makes a quote correct.
1651
1652The build command takes these options: --title, --source, --language en or --language none, --synonyms with a JSON file of word groups, --embed, and with --embed also --model, --dtype, --pooling, --query-prefix, --passage-prefix and --no-map.
1653
1654Exit code · Meaning
1655|---|---|
16560 · Done, or the question was answered.
16571 · The question was refused, lint found something to fix, or eval fell below --min-precision.
16582 · The command line was wrong.
16593 · An input file was missing or invalid.
16604 · Something else failed, such as the model or the disk.
1661
1662### Evaluation
1663
1664npm run eval asks this README a labelled set of questions and reports how often it answers when it should and refuses when it should. Some questions are answerable from the README, and some are not, including questions about nearby topics the README never covers and requests to write something.
1665
1666An answer counts as correct only if one of its quotes contains a passage the question was labelled with. Answer precision is the share of answers that were correct. Answer recall is the share of answerable questions answered correctly. Refusal precision is the share of refusals that were right to refuse. Refusal recall is the share of unanswerable questions that were refused.
1667
1668The thresholds were set by hand while looking only at the development half of the questions. The held-out half was written at the same time and scored once the thresholds were fixed, so it is the fairer measure.
1669
1670Mode · Questions · Answer precision · Answer recall · Refusal precision · Refusal recall
1671|---|---|---|---|---|---|
1672Keywords only, development · 26 · 67% (8/12) · 53% (8/15) · 79% (11/14) · 100% (11/11)
1673Keywords only, held out · 26 · 70% (7/10) · 47% (7/15) · 69% (11/16) · 100% (11/11)
1674Hybrid, development · 26 · 75% (9/12) · 60% (9/15) · 79% (11/14) · 100% (11/11)
1675Hybrid, held out · 26 · 77% (10/13) · 67% (10/15) · 77% (10/13) · 91% (10/11)
1676
1677On answers, the two halves score within a few points of each other; on refusals, the held-out half is lower in both modes. Most wrong answers quote a passage on the right topic that does not answer the question. Most answerable questions that were refused use words the README does not, which meaning search only partly makes up for. Both modes refuse nearly every unanswerable question, and keyword search answers fewer of the answerable ones than hybrid search does.
1678
1679Hybrid results use question embeddings computed in Node and stored in eval/question-vectors.json, so the evaluation runs offline and gives the same numbers every time. A browser can compute slightly different vectors, so its answers can differ at the margins.
1680
1681### Design decisions
1682
1683Quoting instead of generating means every answer can be checked, because every answer is the source. A summary would read better, but a reader would have to trust it.
1684
1685Written answers are opt-in and checked because a fluent answer is easy to trust and hard to verify. Checking every sentence against the record, and striking what fails, keeps the property the quotes have: every claim left on screen points to the line that supports it.
1686
1687Refusing is the default, and a refusal shows the number that fell short and the bar it missed. A refusal with its reasons is as useful as an answer, because it tells the reader the content does not say.
1688
1689Keyword search comes first because it is instant, needs no download, and still works when the model cannot load. Meaning search is added on top of it, never instead of it.
1690
1691A backend is used only after it reproduces the record's own vectors, because WebGPU can run a model and still return wrong numbers on some devices. A backend that fails the check is skipped, and when WebGPU fails it, the browser remembers not to try WebGPU again for that model.
1692
1693Facts are sentence-sized because a quote should be short enough to read at a glance and specific enough to answer one question.
1694
1695The demo marks answers in the README itself, not in a separate answer box, because a quote is easiest to judge in its context, with the sentences around it right there to read.
1696
1697The linter exists because the quality of the answers depends on the writing. A sentence that leans on the one before it is a poor quote, so lint finds those sentences before a visitor does. This README passes its own linter, and a test keeps it that way.
1698
1699Attribution works by occlusion because any embedding model supports it, and its claim is narrow enough to be true: these are the words the similarity depended on. Attribution costs one extra embedding per word of each quoted fact, so it runs only after an asked question is answered, never while typing.
1700
1701Vectors are stored as int8 with one scale per fact, which is a quarter of the size of float32. For 384-dimension unit vectors, the stored vectors keep cosine scores within 0.01 of the originals.
1702
1703Every input from outside the code is parsed before it is trusted: the record, the markdown parser's tokens, the model's output, and the worker's messages.
1704
1705The browser bundle has one runtime dependency, valibot, used to validate the record. The core plus the element is about 27 KB gzipped, without transformers.js, which the worker loads only when it is needed. npm run size, which runs in continuous integration, fails if it grows past 30 KB.
1706
1707### Limits and non-goals
1708
1709Retrieval is not understanding. A quote can share words or meaning with a question without answering it, and the box cannot tell the difference. The reader decides whether a quote answers the question.
1710
1711The answers are only as good as the record. If the record is out of date or wrong, the quotes are too.
1712
1713Keyword search knows English. With --language none, words are matched without stop words or stemming. Chinese, Japanese and other languages written without spaces are not split into words, so keyword search works poorly for them.
1714
1715The thresholds suit all-MiniLM-L6-v2 and records like this README. A different model, or very different content, needs its own thresholds.
1716
1717BM25 ignores word order and negation, so "does not" and "does" look the same to keyword search.
1718
1719Everything is held in memory and every fact is scored for every question, which suits a page or a small set of documents, up to a few thousand facts, not a search engine.
1720
1721The checker is a small NLI model, and it errs both ways: it has kept sentences the README does not support, and struck sentences it does. A kept sentence comes with its score and the line it rests on, as evidence for a reader to weigh, not as a guarantee.
1722
1723Attribution shows sensitivity, not reasoning. An underlined word is one whose removal lowered the similarity, which is not the same as the reason a person would give.
1724
1725The first visit downloads about 29 MB before meaning search is ready: 23 MB of model weights and 6 MB of WebAssembly runtime. Later visits load them from the browser's cache, which took under a second in testing.
1726
1727ask-the-record is not a chatbot: it has no memory of earlier questions, it cannot follow up, and it never writes new text.
1728
1729### Contributing
1730
1731Issues and pull requests are welcome. The checks that run in continuous integration run locally too:
1732
1733```sh
1734npm ci
1735npm audit --audit-level=high
1736npm run licenses
1737npm run typecheck
1738npm run lint
1739npm test
1740npm run build
1741npm run size
1742npx playwright install chromium webkit firefox
1743npm run test:e2e
1744```
1745
1746npm run licenses fails if any dependency is not under MIT, Apache-2.0, BSD or ISC, unless it is a development dependency with a documented reason. Three are documented, and none of them ships: the image library that transformers.js depends on (LGPL-3.0), the CSS tooling inside the test runner (MPL-2.0), and a glob matcher inside the linter (BlueOak-1.0.0).
1747
1748While the local server is up, npm run shots saves a screenshot of every state of both pages, at desktop and phone sizes, into shots/v2/, and remakes demo/og.png from the real page.
1749
1750npm run verify:record records written answers in headless Chromium, with WebGPU, from the models in a shared folder outside the repository; npm run verify:score scores them against the hand labels. Both need a free-space margin of 10 GiB, and neither runs in continuous integration. ATR_LIVE=1 npm run test:e2e -- --project=chromium adds the browser test that loads the real models.
1751
1752npm run eval reruns the evaluation. npm run eval -- --refresh recomputes the question embeddings first, which downloads the model once. After changing this README, run npm run record to rebuild the demo's record, or the tests will fail.
1753
1754A change that adds a guard, such as a limit or a timeout, needs a test that proves the guard triggers. A change to ranking or refusal needs the evaluation rerun and its table above updated.
1755

1761## dreaming
1762
1763
1764Your coding agent proposes changes to its own memory each night; you measure them, check them against everything else it remembers, and review them like a pull request.
1765
1766
1767
1768Coding agents such as Claude Code keep long-term memory as plain files that are loaded into every session. Those files are either written by hand, which goes stale, or written by the agent unsupervised, which accumulates guesses nobody checked. dreaming sits between the two. After you log off, a headless agent with read-only tools re-reads the day's sessions and proposes what memory should learn, correct or forget, citing quotes that dreaming checks against the transcripts. Then dreaming does two things no memory system does for you: it measures a proposal, by running a task suite with and without it in isolated agent sessions and reporting the change in pass rate, turns and tokens with honest intervals; and it checks every proposal for contradictions with the rest of your memory, with a small language-inference model running on your machine. In the morning you approve, edit or reject, with all of that beside each proposal. Only approved changes are written, with a backup and an audit trail. The agent proposes; the evidence is checked; a person approves.
1769
1770### Memory you can measure
1771
1772A memory is an instruction your agent will follow in every session from now on. dreaming treats a proposed one the way you would treat a code change: it runs the tests.
1773
1774```sh
1775dreaming eval prefers-tabs --suite demo/suites/tidepool
1776```
1777
1778The experiment. A task suite is a template repository, a few everyday tasks, and for each task a check the agent never sees. dreaming runs every task the same number of times in two arms: without the proposal (the memory directory as it is now) and with it (the same directory with the proposal applied by the same planner the real apply uses, so the agent sees exactly what approving would write). The arms differ in nothing else: same prompts, same model, same fresh copy of the repository, in a seeded random order so time-of-day drift falls on both. Each run is a real claude -p session; afterwards the task's check decides pass or fail and says why ("ran npm install (1×), which breaks the workspace links"). An eval makes at most 30 runs.
1779
1780The statistics are chosen for small samples, because 30 runs is a small sample:
1781
1782- each arm's pass rate gets the Clopper–Pearson exact interval (Clopper and Pearson, 1934), which never undercovers;
1783- the change in pass rate gets Newcombe's hybrid score interval for a difference of proportions (Newcombe, 1998, method 10), which behaves at 0/5 and 5/5 where the textbook interval collapses (it is tested against the paper's worked examples);
1784- each task is its own comparison, so a task counts as moved only when Fisher's exact test (Fisher, 1922) is below 0.05/k and its interval, made simultaneous at 1 − 0.05/k with a Bonferroni correction (Dunn, 1961), clears zero. With three tasks that is 98.3% each, so a chance "effect" on one of them does not turn up one eval in seven. Both rules were added after the real runs showed why: a tabs memory "helped" a package-manager task by 0/5 → 3/5, and in another batch "hurt" it by 5/5 → 1/5, where the approximate interval clears zero and the exact test (p = 0.048) does not;
1785- turns, tokens and time get a stratified percentile bootstrap of the difference in means (Efron, 1979), resampled within each task, with a seeded generator so a replay prints the same numbers.
1786
1787The approach follows Miller (2024), "Adding Error Bars to Evals": report the interval, not the point; compare arms on the same questions; plan for the sample you can afford. A memory is flagged worse when any task moved down by that rule, and helps when one moved up; otherwise the verdict is "no measurable effect", with the intervals, because that is what five runs per arm per task can say. The pooled interval across tasks is shown for context but does not decide: it mixes tasks with different base rates.
1788
1789What the recorded evals found (synthetic suite, real runs, 2 November 2026):
1790
1791Proposal · Verdict · What moved (98.3% simultaneous CI; exact p) · Per run, with it · Cost, time
1792| -------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------- | -------------- |
1793prefer-pnpm.md, "use pnpm, never npm" · no measurable effect · install-and-test 4/5 → 5/5 (p = 1.0): the baseline already used pnpm, hinted by release-checklist.md · 0.4 fewer turns (95% CI −0.8 to −0.1) · $0.72, 3.7 min
1794prefers-tabs.md, which cites a quote nobody said · ▼ makes high-tide worse · high-tide 5/5 → 0/5 (−100 to −24; p = 0.008): "lint fails: indent with spaces, not tabs" in every run · 7k more tokens (95% CI +3k to +12k) · $0.82, 6.2 min
1795deploy-window.md, "Tuesdays and Thursdays" · ▲ helps on deploy-day · deploy-day 0/5 → 5/5 (+24 to +100; p = 0.008) · 8k more tokens (95% CI +1k to +15k) · $0.79, 7.0 min
1796
1797Focused on the task it is about. Spread over three tasks, prefer-pnpm.md shows no measurable effect, because five runs per arm cannot separate it from a noisy baseline. Run with --tasks install-and-test, all 30 runs measure that one task (15 per arm; 3 November 2026, demo/recorded/focused): install-and-test 5/15 → 15/15, +67 points (95% CI +34 to +85; exact p = 0.0002); per run, 1.5 fewer turns (95% CI −2.3 to −0.6) and 25.8k fewer tokens (95% CI −39.1k to −10.6k); time 71 s → 59 s, an interval that still includes zero (−31 s to +7 s). The eval took 11 minutes and cost $1.35 at API prices, with the same isolation evidence: the control fired, and across the 30 runs there were 0 hook events, 0 canary files and no shim bypass.
1798
1799The same three evals were run three times, 270 real runs in all (the first two batches with an earlier version of the demo memory, and with the memory passed as an argument rather than a file). Under the rule above, every batch gave the same three verdicts. The noisy task is install-and-test: its without-memory pass rate ran from 0/5 to 5/5 between batches, which is why the shipped tabs eval's 5/5 → 1/5 there (p = 0.048) is not called an effect.
1800
1801Isolation, proved rather than assumed. Eval runs must not touch your setup, and your hooks must not run (yours might play sounds). Every run gets --safe-mode (installed plugins, hooks, CLAUDE.md, skills and MCP servers off), --setting-sources project (no user or local settings; the temporary repository has none), --settings with disableAllHooks plus a canary hook on every hook event that would touch a file if any hook ran at all, --strict-mcp-config, --no-session-persistence (no transcript, so no dream ever reads an eval), an environment built from an allowlist (nothing of your session's variables), a working directory outside your home, and the memory in a mode-0600 file (--append-system-prompt-file), never in argv, where any process listing would show it. Then the proof, recorded in every eval:
1802
18031. A positive control. Before any run, Claude Code starts with the canary hook enabled, in an empty, separate config directory (no login, no plugins, no model call). The canary must fire and Claude Code must report the hook events in its stream (--include-hook-events); otherwise the eval refuses to start, because a detector that has not been seen to fire proves nothing by staying silent.
18042. Every run, three independent checks: zero hook events in Claude Code's own stream, no canary file, and zero hooks in its debug log's registry. Any one failing stops the eval.
18053. A process audit, every 200 ms, of every process descended from each agent, flagging sound players (afplay, say, osascript and the like).
18064. The sandbox held: every package-manager command in the agent's Bash calls must reach the suite's shims (real npm sits in /opt/homebrew/bin on macOS and a login shell can put it first); a run where they did not is not counted and stops the eval.
1807
1808In the recorded evals: the positive control fired (SessionStart, UserPromptSubmit and SessionEnd canaries, four hook events) before each eval; across the 90 runs there were 0 hook events, 0 canary files and 0 registered hooks; 97 package-manager commands produced 88 shim calls and no run bypassed the shims; and 4,573 process samples saw no sound player.
1809
1810Writing a suite for your own project takes a directory:
1811
1812```
1813suite.json { "name", "about", "repo", "shims"?, "timeoutSeconds"?, "maxTurns"?,
1814 "tasks": [{ "id", "prompt", "check", "passMeans" }] }
1815repo/ the template repository, copied fresh for every run
1816checks/ one script per task: exit 0 is a pass, the first line it prints is the reason;
1817 it gets EVAL_REPO (the run's copy), EVAL_ANSWER (the agent's final answer)
1818 and EVAL_LOG (every shim call)
1819shims/ optional stand-ins put first on the agent's PATH, for tools a check needs to see used
1820```
1821
1822demo/suites/tidepool is a complete example: three tasks, offline shims for npm, pnpm, npx, yarn and corepack (npm fails exactly as real npm does on pnpm's workspace: protocol), and checks the agent never sees.
1823
1824What an eval cannot tell you. The suite is what it measures: three synthetic tasks written for these memories, so the results are a demonstration of the method, not of Claude in general. Five runs per arm per task detect only large effects; narrow the suite with --tasks to put all 30 runs where the memory matters. Both arms get the memory files appended to the system prompt; Claude Code itself loads the index and reads files on demand, so this is a close stand-in, not the same thing. The cost is real: $0.72 to $0.82 at API prices and four to seven minutes per 30-run eval with Sonnet 5, on a shared and busy laptop, under your own login.
1825
1826### Contradictions across the memory set
1827
1828A new memory can be right and still leave an old one saying the opposite. When the v2 API goes live, "keep the /v1 compatibility tests green" becomes wrong, and an agent told both things will follow whichever it read last. dreaming check (and every dreaming run, when the model is installed) compares each pending proposal, sentence by sentence, with every other memory and every other pending proposal:
1829
18301. sentences from different files are paired when they share at least two content words, a cheap stand-in for "about the same thing", which contradiction requires (de Marneffe, Rafferty and Manning, 2008);

1976### Design decisions
1977
1978The agent never writes. Read-only access is enforced in layers on the claude command line. --restricted confines Claude Code's file tools to the run workspace and the memory directory and ignores user and project settings files, so hooks and plugins configured there do not run. --tools Read,Glob,Grep means no other built-in tool exists in the session; --allowedTools approves only those three; --permission-mode dontAsk denies anything unapproved instead of prompting; --disallowedTools names the built-in tools that write, execute, fetch or delegate, as a backstop; and --strict-mcp-config with no MCP config loads no MCP server. A test asserts the exact argv, and dreaming run --dry-run prints it. The only code that writes to the memory directory is the apply step, and it runs only after a person confirms a diff.
1979
1980Evidence is checked, not trusted. Each quote must appear in a single message of the session it cites, starting and ending on word and character boundaries ("safe to deploy" does not verify against "unsafe to deploy", and a match never splits a letter from its accents or an emoji sequence). Matching ignores differences models introduce when copying (whitespace, typographic quotes and dashes, surrounding quotation marks) and accepts ... between fragments that appear in order within 1,000 characters. Because an elision can drop a word that matters, the reviewer is shown the transcript's own text for the whole matched span, not the agent's rendering of it, together with the transcript line. A proposal with a quote that cannot be found is blocked and cannot be approved without --allow-unverified. Verification proves the quote exists; whether the proposal follows from it is still the reviewer's call.
1981
1982A strict contract, no repair. The reply must be one JSON object matching the schema, either bare or as the only content of a single json code fence. dreaming does not search prose for JSON or patch near-misses: a reply that broke the contract is a run someone should look at. The agent's output (redacted) and the prompt are kept in runs/<run>/, the exit code is non-zero, and the watermark does not move, so the next run retries the same sessions. The output is saved as soon as the agent exits, so a later failure cannot lose a paid reply.
1983
1984A watermark per session, not per run. state.json records each transcript's modification time and number of complete lines when it was last read. A single "last run" timestamp silently loses sessions that were still active during a run, and re-reads whole sessions that were resumed. Per-session marks handle both: active sessions are picked up once they settle, resumed sessions are read from where the last dream stopped, a line still being written is not counted until it is complete, and a run capped by maxSessions leaves the rest for the next one.
1985
1986Never overwrite a person's edits. Each update or delete carries the hash of its target as the agent saw it. If the file has changed since, the proposal is blocked as stale. The apply step re-reads every file just before writing and refuses if anything differs from the diff that was shown. Writes are atomic (temp file, fsync, rename), the memory directory is backed up first, and if any write or the audit append fails, every file already written is restored, any partial audit line is removed, and the error says so.
1987
1988Idempotent by construction. Applying compares the desired end state with what is on disk, rather than replaying a log. Re-applying an applied proposal changes nothing and is recorded as already-applied. That also covers a crash between writing memory and updating the inbox: the next review shows the proposal as already in place and records it.
1989
1990Redaction in both directions. Session text is redacted before the agent sees it, and every free-text string the agent returns (summary, reasons, descriptions, bodies, quotes) is redacted again before it is stored; names and file targets are restricted to slug and file-name shapes. The patterns cover common credential shapes (cloud, model-provider and SaaS API keys, tokens, JWTs, private keys, bearer and basic auth headers, cookies, URL credentials, password=-style assignments) plus long random-looking strings. They favour over-redaction. Quoted values are always redacted in full; an unquoted value that is plainly code is left alone (a type name, a $VAR reference, a read from a well-known root such as process.env, or a function call such as z.string()), since coding sessions are full of them. Every pattern is bounded so a hostile transcript cannot stall a run, and the repository's own files pass the redactor (a test checks). Extra patterns can be added in the config. Redactions in the agent's reply are counted apart from those in the transcripts, and the run says so when there are any: a secret-shaped string the agent wrote is worth knowing about. In review, a proposal that would save a redaction marker into memory is flagged.
1991
1992Transcripts are untrusted input. Sessions can contain text from web pages, files and tool output, including text written to manipulate an agent. The prompt tells the agent that digests are data, not instructions; the agent cannot act on anything it reads; its output is schema-checked; and every change goes past a person. Agent text containing control characters or invisible Unicode (zero-width, bidirectional-override and tag characters) is rejected outright, so nothing can reach a memory file that the reviewer could not see. Terminal output is stripped of escape sequences, and the Markdown inbox puts agent text in code fences, so a previewer never renders an agent-supplied link, image or HTML.
1993
1994dreaming does not dream about itself. The agent runs with --no-session-persistence, and any session whose working directory is inside the dreaming home is skipped, so tomorrow's run does not read tonight's prompt.
1995
1996Small surface. Three runtime dependencies (zod for validation, yaml for frontmatter, diff for unified diffs). There is no TUI framework: the full-screen review writes to the terminal directly (raw keys, the alternate screen, whole-frame redraws), and one review model drives both it and --plain, so tests drive the same decisions through either front end. Confidence is a three-level label rather than a number, because a model's stated probability is not calibrated and a decimal would suggest it is.
1997
1998Any terminal, any width. Every screen is laid out for the terminal it is in. On a narrow one, list columns drop, text wraps at word breaks under its label, and the live clock shortens rather than wrapping (a wrapped line cannot be redrawn in place). Commands and paths are never cut, because a cut command cannot be pasted and run; the dry run prints the agent command one flag per line, and a test feeds it to /bin/sh to prove it reads back as the same arguments. Colour only repeats what the text already says, so with NO_COLOR every mark and word stays and only the highlighting goes. The only thing that moves is the elapsed clock while the agent works.

2088### Limits and non-goals
2089
2090- Confinement is Claude Code's. dreaming relies on Claude Code's restricted mode to keep the agent's file tools inside the workspace and memory directory. The flags were checked against the claude --help of Claude Code 2.1.281 and the constructed command is tested, but the dream itself was never run live: that would mean reading real transcripts. (dreaming eval was run live, on synthetic suites only, under isolation that is proved per run.) Older Claude Code releases may not support every flag; a run then fails with the CLI's error rather than running unconfined.
2091- Restricted mode ignores your settings files. Authentication configured only through settings (an apiKeyHelper, for example) does not apply to the dreaming agent; use your normal login or ANTHROPIC_API_KEY.
2092- Claude Code only, for now. The agent sits behind a small adapter interface (src/agent/adapter.ts: build the command, parse the reply). A Codex adapter (for example codex exec --sandbox read-only) is not implemented.
2093- The transcript format is not a public API. Claude Code's session files are parsed defensively and malformed lines are counted and reported, but a format change could reduce what is read.
2094- Redaction is pattern-based. It will miss a secret with no recognisable shape that is too short or too regular to look random. Add patterns for your own formats.
2095- One memory directory per config. Sessions from every project under the transcripts root feed it.
2096- No retention policy yet. Backups and failed-run workspaces accumulate under ~/.dreaming until you delete them.
2097- macOS and Linux. Windows is untested, and dreaming schedule refuses to run there.
2098- Provenance covers dreaming's own changes. dreaming why knows what the audit log recorded. A memory edited by hand afterwards is reported as changed, but not what changed; a transcript Claude Code has since deleted is reported as gone.
2099- The recording's timing is the recording machine's. The demo plays back at recorded speed with idle gaps capped; on a busy machine the agent and the first frames look slower than they are (the recorder warns when the load is high).
2100- An eval measures its suite. The demo suite was written around the demo's memories; for your own project you write the tasks and checks (a template repo, a prompt, a script that exits 0 for a pass). Five runs per arm per task only detect large effects, and the verdict says so rather than guessing.
2101- Evals cost what Claude costs. Each run is a real claude -p session under your login; the eval reports tokens, time and the API-price cost, and stops at 30 runs.
2102- The contradiction model is small. Precision about 0.82 on the labelled set, which was also used to choose the two-word rule; expect false alarms about the same words in different contexts. It runs in WebAssembly, single-threaded, on the CPU.
2103- Not a memory system. dreaming does not store, retrieve or rank memories; it curates the files your agent already uses.
2104
2105### Contributing
2106
2107```sh
2108npm ci
2109npm run check # typecheck, lint, test, npm audit --audit-level=high
2110npm run demo
2111```
2112
2113CI runs the same steps on Linux (Node 22 and 24) and macOS (Node 22), plus the demo, and renders the recorded screens in Chromium, WebKit and Firefox.
2114
2115The recordings and every screenshot in shots/ come from the real CLI (shots/v2 is kept as v2 left it):
2116
2117```sh
2118npm run record:v3 # shots/v3: eval.svg, loop.svg and stills/<state>-<size>.svg, from a pseudo-terminal
2119npm run shoot -- v3 # each still as a 2x PNG, and og.png (1200×630) for the repository's social preview
2120npm run test:browsers # every SVG in Chromium, then WebKit, then Firefox; two workers, muted (npx playwright install first)
2121node scripts/record-evals.mjs --yes # remake demo/recorded: about 90 real claude -p runs under your login; never in CI
2122```
2123
2124The eval recordings are replays of demo/recorded/evals, labelled as replays on screen; the dream, the simulated failure states (a leaked hook, a logged-out CLI, Ctrl-C) and the review use fake agents that say fake-claude on screen; the contradiction check runs the real model when ~/Personal/.models holds it.
2125
2126scripts/record.mjs runs each scene in a temporary home directory with the fake agent, drives it with keys only once the screen shows what the step waits for, and plays the result through a headless terminal emulator (xterm.js) to draw SVG. In the animated demo each recorded frame is a group shown only for its own slice of the loop, by a stepped CSS animation, so one frame is painted at a time: no script, and a still final frame under prefers-reduced-motion. The text is IBM Plex Mono, embedded in each SVG as a data URI, because an SVG shown as an <img> (as GitHub shows these) may not fetch a font; that is most of each file's weight (eval.svg is 39 KB gzipped, 30 KB of it the two font files), and every run's width is locked to the terminal grid, so the font cannot move the layout. The fonts live in fonts/ with their licence (see THIRD_PARTY.md). There is no web page, so there is no favicon; og.png, the repository's social preview, is a page set in IBM Plex Sans and Sans Condensed from fonts/plex.css, with both faces preloaded, and npm run shoot refuses to write it if a face did not load or anything shifted. TypeScript is strict, ESLint forbids type assertions (data crossing a boundary is parsed with zod instead), and each guard (timeout, limit, validator, redaction rule, lock) has a test that makes it trigger.
2127
2128Two entries in package.json are there for the dependency tree rather than the code: vite is pinned to 7 because vitest would otherwise install vite 8, which brings in an MPL-2.0 package, and the minimatch override moves ESLint's copy past a published advisory. Every package in the tree is MIT, ISC, BSD or Apache-2.0 licensed, except minimatch and one of its dependencies (BlueOak-1.0.0, a permissive licence), which only ESLint uses. The recording tools are development dependencies only: @xterm/headless (MIT) and @playwright/test (Apache-2.0).
2129
2130Use synthetic data only. Never add a real transcript, memory file or credential to the repository, including as a test fixture. Build credential-shaped test strings at runtime from pieces, as the existing tests do; test/repository.test.ts fails if any committed file trips the redactor. A new agent adapter must come with a test that asserts its command is read-only.
